title: Live Comments and Reactions
prompt: Design live comments and emoji reactions for a live video stream. A big stream can have 10 million people watching at once, and they should see comments and reactions roll in as they happen.

clarify.q: How many viewers on the biggest stream, and how many streams in total?
clarify.why: One 10 M-viewer stream is a fan-out problem. A million small streams is a connection and routing problem. The biggest stream sizes the fan-out tree.

clarify.q: Does every viewer need to see every comment?
clarify.why: If not, we can sample. No human reads 20 000 comments a second, and that single answer cuts delivery cost by more than a thousand times.

clarify.q: Must comments appear in the same order for everyone?
clarify.why: A global order needs one ordering point and makes every viewer's feed identical. Relaxing it lets each edge sample and order locally.

clarify.q: Are reactions individual events on screen, or counts and bursts?
clarify.why: Counts can be aggregated per edge per second. Showing each individual reaction would make reactions the biggest load in the system.

clarify.q: Do comments need to be stored and replayed with the recording?
clarify.why: Replay needs durable storage keyed by stream and video time. Live-only would let us skip the database on the delivery path entirely.

clarify.q: How fast must moderation remove a comment everyone has already seen?
clarify.why: Deletes must fan out like comments. 'Within a few seconds' is cheap; 'never visible' means holding every comment until moderation passes.

clarify.q: Which clients: web, mobile, smart TVs?
clarify.why: Mobile on flaky networks reconnects often. TVs may only support long polling. Both shape the edge protocol and reconnect handling.

functional: Viewers post comments on a live stream and see a live feed of other comments.
Viewers send reactions and see aggregated reaction bursts and counts.
A viewer always sees their own comment immediately.
Comments from the streamer and pinned comments reach every viewer.
Moderators and filters can remove comments, and removals reach viewers.
Comments are stored for replay alongside the recording.
nonFunctional: Comment visible to other viewers in p95 under 2 s after posting.
Hold 30 M concurrent connections platform-wide, 10 M on one stream.
Degrade gracefully: under overload show fewer comments, never stall the video or drop connections.
Comment ingestion durable once acknowledged. Delivery is best effort.
Per viewer downstream bandwidth under 2 KB/s for comments and reactions.
outOfScope: Monetized features like paid highlighted comments (mention as an extension).

assumptions: Biggest stream: 10 M concurrent viewers. Platform: 30 M concurrent viewers
Peak write rate on the biggest stream: 20 k comments/s (after a big moment), 200 k reactions/s
One comment message ≈ 200 bytes on the wire, ≈ 300 bytes stored
A viewer can read about 5 comments/s, so we show at most 5/s
One edge server holds 100 k WebSocket connections

steps.label: Fan-out with sampling to 5 per viewer
steps.result: ≈ 10 GB/s ≈ 80 Gbps egress for the biggest stream

steps.label: Edge servers
steps.math: 10 M / 100 k = 100 for the big stream. 30 M / 100 k = 300 platform-wide
steps.result: ≈ 400 edges with headroom. Each sends 100 k × 5 × 200 B = 100 MB/s ≈ 800 Mbps

steps.label: Frames, batched every 500 ms
steps.result: 20 M frames/s total, 200 k frames/s per edge

steps.label: Reactions after edge aggregation
steps.math: 200 k/s raw → each of 100 edges sends one count message per second
steps.result: ≈ 100 messages/s upstream. Counts ride inside the comment frames going down.

steps.label: Comment storage for one event
steps.result: ≈ 16 GB per big event. Small for a wide-column store.

estimates.takeaway: Writes are modest (tens of thousands per second) and fit one ingest pipeline. Delivery is the problem: without sampling it is 2 × 10^11 messages/s. Cap what each viewer sees at about 5 comments/s, aggregate reactions at the edge, and batch frames every 500 ms. That turns it into 80 Gbps spread over roughly 100 edges at 800 Mbps each, which is ordinary hardware.

api.returns: frames { comments[], reactions{ type: count }, removed[], pinned? } every 500 ms
api.note: One socket per viewer. Server-to-client only for the feed; heartbeat every 30 s.
Plain HTTP so writes go through the normal auth, rate limit and abuse stack. clientMsgId dedupes retries.
Fire and forget over the open socket. Edge rate-limits to 5 per second per viewer and aggregates.
Moderators and authors. Emits a removal event through the same fan-out.
Replay by video offset for recorded streams. Served from storage, not the live path.

entities.name: Comment
fields: minute of stream, partition key part
entities.why: Write-heavy and appended in time order. Minute buckets stop a hot stream from creating one enormous partition.

entities.name: Stream topic
entities.store: Kafka, one partition per small-stream group, dedicated partition for big streams
entities.why: Decouples ingest from fan-out and lets the sampler and storage writer consume independently.

entities.name: Edge subscription map
entities.store: Memory on each edge plus a registry (Redis) of stream → edges
entities.why: Relays need to know which edges want a stream so they only forward where viewers are.

data.note: The live path never reads the database. Comments flow ingest → topic → sampler → relays → edges → sockets, all in memory. Storage is a side consumer of the topic, used only for replay, moderation tools and catching up a reconnecting client with the last few seconds. Reaction counts are never stored per event; we store per-second aggregates per stream for replay graphs.

hld.summary:
Writes and reads take different paths. Writes: a comment comes in over HTTP to the comment service, which checks auth and rate limits, runs a fast spam filter, writes it to the stream's topic, and acks. Reads: a sampler per hot stream consumes the topic, drops low-quality comments and forwards a capped stream (say 50/s) to a fan-out tree: regional relays, then edge servers, then viewers' WebSockets. Each edge applies a final per-viewer cap of 5/s and batches every 500 ms.

Reactions travel the other way through the same edges: each edge counts reactions per type per second and sends one small message up to an aggregator, which sums across edges and pushes totals back down the tree. A storage writer consumes the topic to persist comments for replay. Because each layer only talks to tens of children, no single server ever writes to millions of sockets.

diagram.title: Comment ingest and fan-out tree
diagram.src:
flowchart LR
  V1[Viewer posting] --> CS[Comment service]
  CS --> TP[(Stream topic)]
  TP --> SW[Storage writer]
  SW --> DB[(Comment store)]
  TP --> SM[Sampler per hot stream]
  SM --> R1[Regional relay EU]
  SM --> R2[Regional relay US]
  R1 --> E1[Edge servers]
  R2 --> E2[Edge servers]
  E1 --> VW[Viewers]
  E2 --> VW
  E1 --> AG[Reaction aggregator]
  E2 --> AG
  AG --> SM

flows.title: Posting a comment
steps: Client shows the comment in its own feed immediately and POSTs it with a clientMsgId.
Comment service checks auth, per-user rate limit (1 comment per 2 s), and runs the fast filter.
It writes the comment to the stream topic and returns 202 with visible or held.
Sampler reads it, scores it, and either forwards it to relays or drops it from the live feed. It is still stored for replay.

flows.title: Receiving the feed
steps: Viewer opens a WebSocket to the nearest edge. Edge registers interest in the stream with its regional relay if it is the first local viewer.
Relay forwards the sampled stream (about 50/s) to every subscribed edge.
Every 500 ms the edge builds a frame per viewer: up to 2–3 comments from the buffer, current reaction totals, and any removals.
Slow sockets get frames dropped, never queued: the next frame replaces the old one.

flows.title: Sending a reaction
steps: Viewer taps heart. Client animates locally and sends react over the socket.
Edge increments an in-memory counter for (stream, heart) and enforces 5 per second per viewer.
Once a second the edge sends its counts to the aggregator and resets them.
Aggregator sums across edges and pushes totals down the tree. Clients animate a burst sized by the change.

deepDives.title: The fan-out tree
deepDives.problem: One publisher cannot send to 10 M sockets or even to 400 edges with low and even latency. Each hop also adds delay, and the tree must change shape as viewers move between streams.

options.name: Pub/sub broker, every edge subscribes
options.how: Edges subscribe to a channel per stream in Redis pub/sub or similar. Sampler publishes once; the broker copies to each subscriber.
pros: Simple, few moving parts
Fine for streams with a handful of edges
cons: One channel with hundreds of subscribers puts all copying on one broker node
Broker node failure cuts a whole stream

options.name: Two-level tree: sampler → regional relays → edges
options.how: Sampler sends to about 10 relays (one per region or zone). Each relay sends to the edges in its region that have viewers. Edges register and unregister with their relay.
pros: Each node has few children: 10 relays, about 10–40 edges each
Cross-region traffic is one copy per region
Relays are stateless and easy to replace
cons: One extra hop (a few ms)
Membership must be maintained as edges come and go

options.name: Everything through Kafka consumers
options.how: Each edge consumes the stream's topic partition directly.
pros: Durable, replayable
cons: Hundreds of consumers on one partition pull raw unsampled data
Consumer group churn as edges scale is slow

deepDives.choice: Pub/sub for small streams, a two-level tree for big ones. Most streams have a few viewers on a few edges, so a shared broker channel is fine. When a stream crosses roughly 50 k viewers, it gets a dedicated sampler and the relay tree: sampler fan-out is about 10, relay fan-out about 10–40, and the hot stream's 100 edges each get the same 50 comments/s, about 5 000 messages/s through the tree. If the biggest stream grew to 100 M viewers I'd add one more relay level rather than widening any node.

deepDives.title: WebSocket edge servers
deepDives.problem: Edges hold millions of long-lived connections. They must survive slow mobile clients, restarts and deploys, and a goal in a football match that makes 10 M people react at once, without one slow socket blocking others or a reconnect storm melting the system.

options.name: WebSockets with per-connection drop-oldest buffers
options.how: Edge keeps a tiny outbound buffer per socket (one or two frames). If a frame is still unsent when the next is ready, replace it.
pros: Memory per connection bounded to a few KB
Slow clients degrade alone
cons: Slow clients miss comments, which is acceptable here

options.name: Server-sent events or long polling fallback
options.how: One-way HTTP stream, with reactions and posts sent over normal HTTP.
pros: Works through strict proxies and on some TVs
Simple HTTP infrastructure
cons: Reactions over HTTP cost a request each unless batched on the client
Long polling adds latency

deepDives.choice: WebSockets with drop-oldest buffers as the default, with SSE as a fallback. Event-loop servers hold 100 k sockets each at a few KB per connection. To avoid reconnect storms: clients reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter (first retry 1–5 s, random); deploys drain an edge over minutes, telling clients to reconnect elsewhere at random times; the load balancer spreads by least connections. On reconnect the client sends lastSeenId, and the edge sends the last few seconds from its in-memory buffer instead of hitting storage. If edges ran hot, the first lever is a longer frame interval (1 s instead of 500 ms), not more servers.

deepDives.title: Sampling and ranking comments
deepDives.problem: At 20 k comments/s, someone must decide which few each viewer sees. Random sampling surfaces spam and repeats. Strict top-N ranking makes the feed identical for everyone and hides most people's comments forever.

options.name: Random sample at each edge
options.how: Edge keeps a buffer and picks randomly each frame.
pros: Cheap, fair spread of exposure
cons: Low-quality and spam comments shown as often as good ones

options.name: Score at the sampler, weighted sample at the edge
options.how: Sampler scores each comment (spam probability, account age, length, duplicates, language) and forwards the top ~50/s. Edges then pick per viewer with probability weighted by score, plus always-include rules.
pros: Better quality
Different viewers see different comments, so more comments get seen
Cheap: scoring is once per comment, not per viewer
cons: Scoring adds a few hundred milliseconds
Tuning the score is product work

options.name: Fully personalized feed per viewer
options.how: Rank per viewer using their friends, language and history.
pros: Most relevant
cons: Per-viewer ranking at 50 M deliveries/s is expensive
Needs user data at the edge

deepDives.choice: Score once, sample per viewer at the edge. Always-include rules: your own comments (echoed locally), the streamer's, moderators', and pinned ones. Light personalization is cheap if it is coarse: the edge can prefer comments in the viewer's language using a tag on the comment. When the raw rate is low (a small stream with 3 comments/s), sampling is off and everyone sees everything. I'd add per-viewer friend boosting only if product data showed it raised engagement, since it requires shipping social graph data to edges.

deepDives.title: Aggregating reactions
deepDives.problem: 200 k reactions/s on one stream. Sending each one up to a central counter and each one down to viewers would make reactions the largest traffic in the system, for something people perceive as a vibe, not a list.

options.name: Central counter, every reaction an increment
options.how: Edges send each reaction to Redis INCR on a key per stream and type.
pros: Exact counts
cons: 200 k increments/s on one key is a hot key on one shard
Every edge talks to one Redis node

options.name: Edge pre-aggregation every second
options.how: Edge counts locally, sends one message per second with per-type counts. Aggregator sums and broadcasts totals down the tree.
pros: Upstream traffic drops from 200 k/s to about 100/s
Down traffic piggybacks on comment frames
cons: Up to about 2 s of delay for counts
Counts are approximate if an edge dies before flushing

deepDives.choice: Edge pre-aggregation. Exactness does not matter for a heart counter; the felt latency of a burst is about 1–2 s, which this meets. The client animates its own tap instantly, so the user never waits. For a paid reaction (a tip or gift) I would not use this path: it must go through the payment system and show as an individual, durable event.

deepDives.title: Who sees what: the consistency trade-off
deepDives.problem: Two viewers side by side will see different comments, in slightly different order, and a deleted comment may stay on screen for a second. Is that acceptable, and what must be strict?

options.name: Same feed for everyone
options.how: A single global sequence, sampled once centrally. Every edge shows exactly the same comments in the same order.
pros: Easy to reason about, screenshots match
Removal is exact: one place decides
cons: Only 5 comments/s get any exposure, the rest of 20 k/s are never seen by anyone
Central sampler is a single bottleneck

options.name: Per-edge or per-viewer sampling, eventually consistent
options.how: Each viewer sees a different sample. Order is by server timestamp within the edge buffer.
pros: Spreads exposure across many more comments
No global coordination
cons: No two feeds match
Removals race with display

deepDives.choice: I'd guarantee three things and relax the rest. Strict: read-your-writes (your comment shows instantly, rendered locally and deduped by clientMsgId when it comes back); streamer and pinned comments reach everyone; removals propagate within about 2 s through the same tree and edges also drop removed ids from their buffers. Relaxed: which comments you see, and order across edges. If the product needed 'never visible before moderation' (for example a children's platform), I would hold every comment until moderation passes and accept 1–3 s more latency.

failures: An edge server dies, dropping 100 k sockets
Clients reconnect with jittered backoff to other edges. Others absorb about 1% more load each. Relay removes the dead edge from its list on heartbeat timeout.
A big moment causes 10× comment volume
Ingest is rate-limited per user; sampler keeps its forward cap at 50/s, so downstream load does not change. The extra comments are only stored.
Sampler for a hot stream crashes
A standby sampler consumes the same topic from the last committed offset. Feed pauses for a few seconds; video and reactions continue.
Score drops new-account comments to near zero in sampling; tighten per-user and per-IP limits; hold comments from accounts under 1 day old.
Edges subscribe to a second relay in the region. Sampler sheds load by lowering its forward cap before relays fall over.
No effect on the live feed. Replay is delayed; the topic retains 24 h so the writer catches up.
scale: 10× viewers on one stream: 1 000 edges; add a third tree level so no relay feeds more than about 50 edges. Per-viewer bandwidth stays the same.
10× comment rate: partition ingest for that stream by commentId hash; the sampler becomes several scorers feeding one merger. Downstream unchanged.
Millions of small streams: pack many streams per topic partition and use broker pub/sub only; trees exist just for the top few hundred streams.
Cost pressure: lower the cap from 5 to 3 comments/s under load, which cuts comment egress by 40% (3/5 = 60% remains), and raise the frame interval to 1 s to halve frame count.

followups.q: How would you show 'X people are watching'?
answer: Each edge reports its connection count per stream every few seconds.
Aggregator sums and broadcasts the total with reaction counts.
Rounded display (1.2 M) hides noise; exactness is not needed.

followups.q: How do you sync comments with the video for replay?
answer: Store offsetMs from the stream start, taken from the viewer's player position when posting, corrected by known latency.
Replay fetches comments by time window as the video plays.
Live viewers are 5–30 s behind real time, so ordering by server time alone would put comments before the moment they react to.

followups.q: What if the streamer wants to see every comment?
answer: Streamer's dashboard reads the unsampled topic for their stream through a dedicated consumer.
Still capped by what a person can read, so add filters: questions only, subscribers only, keyword search.
This is one client, so cost is negligible.

followups.q: How do you stop one user from flooding?
answer: Per-user rate limit on posts (token bucket, for example 1 per 2 s, burst of 3).
Per-connection reaction cap at the edge.
Duplicate detection in the scorer drops repeated text.

followups.q: Why not use HTTP polling every second?
answer: 10 M viewers polling once a second is 10 M requests/s with full HTTP overhead.
Most responses would carry the same sampled content.
WebSockets push one 500 ms frame with no request overhead, and polling can stay as a fallback.

mistakes: Fanning out every comment to every viewer without doing the 2 × 10^11 math.
Writing each reaction to a central counter or database.
Putting a database read on the live delivery path.
Queuing unbounded data for slow sockets instead of dropping stale frames.
Promising every viewer an identical, complete, ordered feed.

mid: Used WebSockets (or SSE) for delivery and HTTP for posting
Stored comments separately from the live delivery path
Asked whether every viewer must see every comment
senior: Computed naive fan-out and capped per-viewer delivery with a number
Built a fan-out tree or pub/sub layer so no node writes to millions of sockets
Aggregated reactions at the edge and piggybacked counts on frames
Handled slow clients with bounded buffers and reconnects with jitter
Stated which consistency guarantees are strict (own comment, removals) and which are relaxed
staff: Used different strategies for small and huge streams and named the threshold
Described graceful degradation levers in order (frame interval, cap, sampling) before adding capacity
Separated paid reactions onto a durable path
Linked replay timing to stream latency
